newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria says will not allow oil output disruption.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria says will not allow oil output disruption.

text.p: Oil minister Dan Etete warned on Wednesday that Nigeria's military government would not tolerate disruption of crude oil activities because of communal feuds.
"The present administration will not tolerate a situation where every political grievance is taken out on the oil installations and operations of oil companies," Etete said.
He was speaking at the start of a three-day seminar on relations between oil companies and their host communities.
Multinational oil company executives, oil-producing community leaders and state oil company officials were attending the seminar which ends on Friday.
Crude oil is the economic engine of Nigeria, accounting for slightly more than 90 percent of its foreign exchange earnings.
But ethnic feuds, especially in the riverine areas of the Niger delta where most of Nigeria's oil is produced, are rife.

The most recent are continuing clashes between armed youths of Ijaw and Itsekiri tribes in the oil town of Warri since March 22 that have affected oil production by Royal Dutch Shell Group's Nigerian unit.
Shell pumps about 950,000 barrels per day (bpd) of the nation's two million bpd.

At the height of the March crisis, armed Ijaw tribesmen occupied six Shell oil flow stations, shutting a total of 100,000 bpd, while another 110,000 bpd was shut in southeastern Nembe creek due to a similar feud by two communities.
A total of 127 of Shell's Nigerian staff held hostage by the Ijaw tribesmen were released in batches following delicate negotiations before crude oil production could resume.
Etete told community leaders to restrain their youths, whom he said had the habit of vandalising equipment and machines of oil companies.
"Host communities should relate with operators in the oil industry as frequent unrests in the oil-producing communities are not conducive to sustainable development," he said.

He said oil multinationals should be "socially responsible citizens." He added, "Oil companies' profits should be re-invested in these communities to alleviate the negative impact of their operations."
Oil-producing communities often complain that the oil activities of the multinationals were damaging their environment and have been seeking compensations in return.
